blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — AV fistula/graft cannulation using site antisepsis and aseptic vascular-access technique
stem: A nurse performs hand hygiene before cannulating a client's arteriovenous fistula for hemodialysis. Which additional infection-prevention action best reflects CDC dialysis guidance?

options.A: Prepare the access site with skin antiseptic, allow it to dry, avoid re-touching the prepared site, and insert the fistula needles aseptically.
options.B: Put on new clean gloves and cannulate after soap-and-water cleansing alone when the fistula skin looks intact, because visible cleanliness is sufficient.
options.C: Use sterile gloves and a sterile drape, then palpate the prepared site with the same gloves before needle insertion to confirm the vessel position.
options.D: Use clean technique for fistula cannulation after hand hygiene, reserving aseptic access practices for clients who have a dialysis catheter.

rationale: A is correct. CDC dialysis-safety resources emphasize staff competency in vascular-access care and aseptic technique. The CDC AV fistula/graft cannulation checklist specifies cleansing the access site, performing hand hygiene, putting on new clean gloves, applying skin antiseptic and allowing it to dry, avoiding contact with the site after antisepsis, inserting needles aseptically, and connecting to blood lines aseptically. B is incorrect because soap-and-water cleansing does not replace the skin-antiseptic step in the checklist. C is incorrect because touching the prepared site after antisepsis conflicts with the no-contact step even if sterile gloves are worn. D is incorrect because aseptic access practices are not limited to dialysis catheters; CDC maintains specific aseptic cannulation tools for AV fistulas and grafts.
educational_objective: Use skin antisepsis and aseptic cannulation every time an AV fistula or graft is accessed for hemodialysis, in addition to hand hygiene and clean gloves.

option_audit.A: Correct; matches the CDC cannulation checklist's skin-antisepsis, drying, no-re-touch and aseptic needle-insertion steps.
option_audit.B: Plausible clean-access shortcut; incorrect because soap-and-water cleansing alone does not replace skin antisepsis before cannulation.
option_audit.C: Plausible sterile-barrier approach; incorrect because re-touching the prepared site conflicts with the CDC no-contact step after antisepsis.
option_audit.D: Plausible catheter-focused misconception; incorrect because CDC applies aseptic cannulation practices to AV fistulas/grafts as well.
